description: Use ONLY when the user asks to write comments or annotation marks into the game. For why someone lost or turning points use explain_game_result instead. Annotate the game on the board: classify every move with the chess engine, then write a comment for the moves that deserve one (blunders, mistakes, inaccuracies, and the only move that holds). With 'prose' true (the default) the comment is written by the language model from the engine's facts and checked; with 'prose' false the comment is the engine's own verdict in words, which costs no model call. 'marks' also sets the standard annotation mark. 'max_plies' bounds the work; 'from_move' and 'to_move' annotate only that stretch ('analyse moves 20 to 30'). The game is left modified for the user to save.

max_plies.description: stop after this many moves, default 60

to_move.description: annotate up to and including this move number

tool_menu_hint: ask the chess engine about a position

description: Quick read-only chess-engine pass over the current game's mainline. Prefer this for 'why did White/Black lose', 'why did I lose', 'where did it go wrong', and 'what was the turning point', including follow-ups. Returns up to three biggest evaluation drops for the losing side, numbered moves played, better moves and evaluations before/after. Default side is the loser from the recorded result; select white or black when requested. Evaluations are short-search estimates, not proof of a tactical cause. Give friendly coaching in at most four short sentences: lead with the turning-point story, use SAN moves and evaluations in words, omit engine numbers unless asked, and end with one useful offer. Never infer a tactical cause from an evaluation drop alone; do not annotate or create another game.
name: explain_game_result

side.description: side to explain; default auto (recorded loser)

tool_menu_hint: find this game's turning points without changing it

tool_menu_hint: fact-check the annotations of this game

tool_menu_hint: find a video lesson for this position

description: Find positions, patterns or tactics in the active database's games with Chesswiz's CQL 6.2 engine. When search_games has the pattern (its 'pattern' list: named mates, forks, the Greek gift, the 7th rank, outposts, pawn structures, Lucena and other endgames), use search_games instead: those searches are vetted and fast. You translate the request into a CQL 6.2 script; CQL decides what matches. Put only the positional part in 'cql', starting with cql() (e.g. 'cql() mate', 'cql() flipcolor {move from N} attacks k'); put names, colour, result, dates, event, ECO and Elo in the other fields, which narrow the games before any is read. Call cql_help first for the CQL 6.2 reference and worked examples unless the script is trivial. Step 1: mode sample (the default) returns up to 3 matching positions (the move that led there, the game, the FEN) and shows them to the user as diagrams in the Report pane; tell the user in one sentence what you searched for and ask whether these are what they meant. Step 2, only after the user agrees: call again with mode all and the same arguments; the game list then shows every matching game. If the script does not parse you get the parser's message: fix it and call again. Never describe a position's quality yourself.
name: find_positions

request.description: what the user asked for, in their words

cql.description: the CQL 6.2 script for the positional part, starting with cql()

mode.description: sample (default): up to 3 positions to check with the user; all: every match, shown in the game list

min_elo.description: minimum average Elo of the two players

both_min_elo.description: minimum Elo of each player: both players rated at least this

description: Find games with positions like the one on the board ('games like this one', 'similar positions') in the active database; the application writes the CQL 6.2 search, so no cql_help is needed. 'aspects' says what must be alike: pawns (the pawn structure, both sides), material (the same pieces), pieces (kings and pieces on the same squares); default pawns alone. The game on the board is left out of the results. 'tolerance' lets up to 0, 1 or 2 pawns per side stand elsewhere (default 0). 'colours' both also finds the structure with the colours reversed. Same two steps as find_positions: mode sample first (the user sees diagrams and the search in the Report pane; ask whether that is what they meant), then mode all. Header fields narrow the games first.
name: find_similar

tolerance.description: 0, 1 or 2 pawns per side may stand elsewhere

min_elo.description: minimum average Elo of the two players

both_min_elo.description: minimum Elo of each player: both players rated at least this

tool_menu_hint: find positions like the one on the board

name: switch_tab

description: The exact result of an endgame with at most 7 pieces (kings included) from the Syzygy tablebases, looked up online at Lichess (only the position is sent): win, draw or loss for the side to move, mate distance, and which moves win, draw or lose. The board position, or 'fen'. Prefer it to the engine for such endgames: it is perfect play, not an estimate.
name: tablebase

description: The pending [after] timers (id, kind, script) and the open channels of the interpreter. Use it for a busy or frozen GUI and for leaked timers.
name: timers
tool_menu_hint: list pending timers and open channels

description: The most recent assistant tool calls of this session, newest last: time, tool, arguments, whether the user was asked, outcome (ok, error, declined) and the start of the reply. Use it to explain what the assistant did or why something failed.
name: tool_log

description: Build puzzles from the active database's games: Chesswiz's CQL matcher finds positions just before a decisive move: a checkmate (any, or a smothered, back-rank, Boden's, Anastasia's, Arabian, epaulette or queen-and-pawn mate), a Legal's or Blackburne's mate, a double or discovered check, a knight or pawn fork, a skewer, a double attack on loose pieces, a pinned piece attacked by a pawn, a Greek gift or double bishop sacrifice, or an underpromotion; by default a mix of all. The chess engine keeps only those whose solution is its best move and clearly the only good one. The puzzles are written to a PGN file under the user directory, which the user can open as a database to train. 'pattern' limits it to one kind; 'player' to one player's games; 'max' bounds the number of puzzles (default 20). It runs in the background; the Report pane shows the progress and the result.
name: training_set

max.description: at most this many puzzles, default 20

tool_menu_hint: build a training set from the games of the database

description: The transcript of a media file (the speech of an audio lesson or a video), as plain text, from the local speech-to-text engine. Read-only; nothing is stored. Use it when the user asks what is said in a lesson, or wants its text. Long transcripts are cut; the answer starts with a short summary.
name: transcribe_media

description: Have the error log triaged now: new error groups are classified (bug, environment, user, noise) and every bug gets an issue file. Runs in the background; the result is posted here when it is done.
name: triage_errors

description: The toplevel windows (state, geometry, title), the focus and the grab holder. A grab held by a window that is not showing or by a menu button whose menu is not posted is flagged as stuck: that is what makes a GUI ignore mouse clicks while menus still work.
name: ui_state
tool_menu_hint: inspect the windows, focus and grab

description: Fetch FIDE's current rating list from ratings.fide.com and install it as Chesswiz's player data: names, FIDE IDs, federations, titles, birth years and standard ratings of the players rated 1800 or more (or titled). Player cards and name lookups then use it. Use it when the user asks to update ratings or player data, or when a player's federation, title or rating looks out of date. It downloads from the internet, so the user is asked first.
name: update_player_data
tool_menu_hint: download FIDE's current rating list (about 45 MB) and update the player data

description: Whether speaking to the assistant is available: the recorder, the local speech-to-text engine and model, and how replies are spoken. Use it when the user asks about voice input, dictation, or why the microphone button is not there.
name: voice_status
